catalog_quote: Mead 1998:97 (sec. 3.1.2 Syllable patterns and stress): 'I assume that in Proto-Bungku-Tolaki stress fell on the penultimate syllable, there being no reason to reconstruct otherwise. All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages also exhibit penultimate stress.' Mead 1999:101-102 (Appendix 3, word lists incl. Bungku): '(g) In the absence of any stress marking, one can assume penultimate stress occurring on the next to last written vowel. ... (d) None of the Bungku-Tolaki languages have phonemically long vowels. Phonetically long vowels are nearly always a reflection of two vowels of the same quality, and have been transcribed as such in the following data ... All of the Bungku-Tolaki languages may be considered open syllable languages, with the only syllable patterns being V and CV.'

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding quotations are verbatim in copies we hold at the stated places (Mead 1998 p.97 page scan + scanned l.344-348; Mead 1999 l.5193-5227). (2) The classification (fixed penultimate) rests on a 1998 dissertation by the family's main specialist, but the sentence is a family-wide blanket claim, not a description of Bungku; Mead 1999's word-list convention is a transcription default. (3) Web/archive search found one Bungku-specific stress description, Adriani 1900:261 (MNZG 44), downloaded from archive.org and read on the page scan: base and derived words have penultimate stress, stress shifts rightward when suffixes (incl. pronominal -ngku/-mu, and the kinitángku.. kinita míu paradigm) attach, and a few oxytones result from vowel contraction (pená < penawa, wulá < wulawa; these are final VV under Mead's transcription, hence still 'next-to-last written vowel')
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again: independently re-done, all confirmed. sources.quote: p.261: 'De klemtoon verspringt bij aanhechting van suffixen. Grondwoorden hebben den klemtoon op de voorlaatste lettergreep, samengestelde woorden evenzoo, onverschillig waar het grondwoord dien had. Bijv. úlu "hoofd", ulúngku "mijn hoofd", ulúmu "uw hoofd", mongkíta "zien", kinitángku "door mij gezien"; nináhu "gekookt", inahúo "te koken". Een oxytonisch accent, waarvan enkele voorbeelden hier volgen, is gewoonlijk 't gevolg van samentrekking, bijv.: owú "kruin van 't hoofd", uit wu(w)u; pená "adem" uit pena(w)a; olontú "knie" ...; wulá "goud" uit wula(w)a. In kiná "gekookte rijst" is de klem
sources.locator: p. 261 'Woordvorm en klemtoon' (p. 274); also the -in- passive paradigm note a few pages later ( l.23901)

sources.note: Purely segmental: 10 vowel phones but 5 vowel phonemes /i a e o u/ (long vowels [a: i: u: e: o:] are non-phonemic allophones - 'the short and long sound.. does not disturb or influence the meaning'), 18 consonant phonemes, prenasalized clusters, no word-final consonants ('vocalic language'), distinctive-feature characterization whose 'Features of Prosody' lists [+stress]: '-' (none) and [-stress]: all vowels.
